analysis.one_liner: Lets state attorneys general sue police departments for patterns of unconstitutional misconduct and expands federal enforcement funding.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the House and died at the end of the 117th Congress, with no Republicans among its cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under existing law, only the Justice Department can sue a state or local police agency for a pattern or practice of unconstitutional conduct, such as systematic excessive force or discrimination, and those cases usually end in a consent decree, a court-enforced agreement to change how the department works. This bill would also let state attorneys general bring those federal cases, with safeguards to keep officials from investigating their own governments. It would add money for Justice Department civil rights enforcement and for state investigations, and require consent decrees to include community oversight bodies made up of people who have never worked in law enforcement, plus non-police remedies like mental health support and restorative justice.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live in jurisdictions with documented patterns of police misconduct benefit: communities harmed by unconstitutional policing, residents who would gain a community oversight body with authority to question the agency and demand records, and people in crisis who would be met with mental health and social work responses instead of police. State attorneys general gain a new enforcement tool, and the DOJ Civil Rights Division gains dedicated funding.

how_it_helps.text: It lets state attorneys general bring federal civil cases against law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and courts engaged in patterns or practices of unconstitutional conduct, adding a second front of enforcement beyond the Justice Department and reducing reliance on federal priorities.

It includes conflict-of-interest safeguards: a state official inside the jurisdiction under investigation cannot be designated to investigate it, and statewide investigations must be run by an independent organization unaffiliated with government.

It authorizes $445 million per year for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, with at least $100 million per year reserved for pattern-or-practice enforcement and technical assistance, and $150 million per year in grants to states, which may fund social workers and behavioral health crisis experts to reduce dependence on police.

It requires consent decrees to include community oversight bodies made up of people who have never worked in law enforcement, with authority to question the agency, obtain its records, and recommend changes.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the cost of up to $595 million per year in authorized federal spending. Police departments, prosecutors' offices, and courts found to have engaged in patterns of unconstitutional conduct bear the cost of litigation, court-ordered reforms, and community oversight requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes up to $595 million per year in new federal spending ($445 million for the DOJ Civil Rights Division plus $150 million for state grants, for each of fiscal years 2021 through 2030), which falls on taxpayers and competes with other uses of public money.

State and local law enforcement agencies, prosecutors, and courts found to have engaged in patterns of unconstitutional conduct would face federal litigation, court-ordered reforms, and ongoing oversight by community bodies with authority to demand documents and question officials.

A good-faith objection is that expanding litigation authority and steering consent decrees toward non-law-enforcement remedies does not directly guarantee reduced crime or reduced misconduct; results depend on how well state attorneys general and community oversight bodies actually perform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial for communities that have been the subject of Justice Department findings of systemic police misconduct: more investigators, more enforcement channels, and consent decrees that require community oversight and non-police remedies. The costs are real but bounded: up to $595 million per year in authorized federal spending, and a heavier compliance burden on police departments, prosecutors, and state governments that are found to have engaged in unlawful patterns or practices. The state-enforcement provision is designed with safeguards against conflicts of interest, which addresses the most obvious objection (a state attorney general suing itself). A fair criticism is that more litigation and federal money do not by themselves guarantee better policing, and the bill would have required sustained annual appropriations that authorization bills do not guarantee. On balance, the design is serious and targeted at a documented enforcement gap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee when it was introduced, later routed to two of its subcommittees, and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 4, 2021 and referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day.

On November 1, 2022, five months before the Congress ended, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties and to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, but no further action followed.
The bill had a Democratic sponsor and 16 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and state and local governments that would have faced pattern-or-practice suits and consent decrees are better off, since no additional enforcement or oversight was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies facing no new oversight

for.name: 16 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jerrold Nadler, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing or committee vote; after more than a year it was only routed to two subcommittees in November 2022, and the Congress ended with no further action.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with the House taking no action the bill never reached a vote that could have tested broader support.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill exposes police departments, prosecutors, and courts to pattern-or-practice suits by state attorneys general as well as the Justice Department, and to consent decrees with community oversight bodies empowered to demand records and recommend changes. Departments with records of systemic misconduct would face binding reform.

industries.industry: Mental health and community-based social services
industries.note: Consent decrees would be required to consider remedies such as mental health support and restorative justice, and state grants could fund social workers and behavioral health crisis experts, creating funding for providers of these services.
